# Why Cáishén is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *caishen*. This is the file on how **Cáishén** replaced it.

Cáishén's mythology is young and openly composite. The cult is a Song-dynasty growth over older roots, and every avatar brings his own story: a Ming novel supplies the marshal, a Han historian the heartless minister, merchants the retired sage. The tradition never pretends otherwise — and its honesty is part of its power.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Cáishén
- **ASCII form:** caishen
- **Meaning:** "God of wealth"
- **Domain of influence:** Wealth, Prosperity, New Year
- **Pantheon:** Chinese
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 財神
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 99 of 546

## The Name Before the Marks

The name is attested as **財神**, as Fengshen Yanyi (Investiture of the Gods, Ming) and Santjiao soushen daquan (Yuan–Ming compendium) record. On the evidence, it means "God of wealth".

Strip **Cáishén** to *caishen* and 2 pieces of evidence vanish:

- **a → á** — Acute tone mark: the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.
- **e → é** — Acute tone mark: the stress position the ASCII form cannot show.

A reader who knows the marks hears the name correctly on the first try. A reader who never sees them never gets the chance.

Spoken, the name runs `/caishen/` — 'CAISHEN' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Cáishén** lives at [/caishen/](/caishen/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/caishen/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/caishen/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/caishen/patterns/).

Tier-1 is not a compliment; it is a measurement. This restoration keeps something the ASCII form provably loses, and the measurement is repeatable.

## Where the Name Stood First

The material record of Cáishén is popular, mass-produced, and deliberately ephemeral — which is itself testimony. Late-imperial woodblock New Year prints (nianhua) from Yangliuqing (Tianjin), Taohuawu (Suzhou), and Mianzhu (Sichuan) turned out hundreds of thousands of red-and-gold god-images each winter, to be pasted above doorways and burned in the fourth-night send-off. The Yuan–Ming god-compendium Santjiao soushen daquan reached households in cheap woodblock editions that carried the mythology to the non-literate. Wealth-god shrines stand in guild halls and temples across the Sinosphere, usually flanked by his assistants with the tiger at his feet; paper and porcelain icons still sit on shop altars everywhere, replaced annually — wealth itself made a renewable rite. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **6 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Finance, Wealth & Commerce** (the Chinese god of wealth whose image appears in shops, homes, and businesses during the New Year.); **Mythic Name Restoration** (the Chinese god of wealth in toned pinyin.); **Retail & Marketplaces** (the god of wealth is the patron of merchants; his image hangs in shops and market stalls across the Chinese diaspora.).
